newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israelis wary of visiting Jordan after attack.
newsitem.headline: Israelis wary of visiting Jordan after attack.

text.p: The soldier who gunned down seven Israeli schoolgirls in north Jordan last week also dealt a blow to Jordan's vital tourism sector, travel agents and hotels said on Tuesday.
Many groups, mainly from Israel, cancelled outright or cut their numbers because of the border attack, which occurred just as Jordan's tourist industry was gearing up for its springtime high season.

"I called 15 travel agents and most of them were crying," said a hotel sales representative at the ancient rock city of Petra, Jordan's most famous tourist site. "At minimum they have four or five groups each which cancelled, mostly Israelis."
"I had one group cut from 45 people to 17 after the shooting," he added.
Around 110,000 of the 1.10 million tourists who visited Jordan last year were Israelis and the money they spent added crucial foreign currency to Jordan's economy.
Hotel officials said growing tension between neighbouring Israel and the Palestinians had already cast a shadow on business before the Jordanian soldier's attack.

Jordanian army driver Sergeant Ahmed Mousa Mustafa al-Daqamsa emptied the clip of his rifle on Thursday at the Israeli girls on a school trip to a strip of Jordanian land south of the Sea of Galilee leased to Israel under a 1994 peace treaty. He was arrested.

"We have been receiving cancellations since February," said the reservations manager at another Petra hotel. "I don't think there is anything new since (the attack), but in March we're meant to be full and today we only have 70 percent occupancy."

Jordan hopes for a 15 percent increase in tourist arrivals this year after a disappointing 2.8 percent rise in 1996, when tourists were discouraged by a wave of violence in the Middle East including car bombs in Israel, Israeli military strikes on Lebanon, fighting in the West Bank and bread riots in Jordan.

Revenues last year rose around 10 percent to $770 million, a modest increase compared to the $500 million which Jordan says has been invested in hotels and transport since it signed a 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
Some travel agents played down the lower hotel occupancy, saying it was caused by the optimistic wave of new hotel building since 1994.
"There are bound to be a few cancellations," said one. "But the difference now is just the number of hotels... Petra used to have three or four big hotels, now it has 13."
Another six large hotels are expected to be built in Amman by next year.

Tourism Minister Saleh Irsheidat said there had been an immediate fall in numbers after Thursday's shooting but said a visit to Israel by King Hussein had reassured both Israelis and tourists from further afield.
"Maybe for the first few days we noticed a drop," he told Reuters. "But now it is behind us." He said border crossings at the southern Eilat-Aqaba checkpoint with Israel were back to normal.
